# backloop.dev — discontinued

> backloop.dev provided free HTTPS on localhost: every subdomain of `*.backloop.dev` resolves to `127.0.0.1` and `::1`, and the site published a publicly trusted wildcard certificate for `*.backloop.dev` that anyone could download. The service was discontinued on 2026-09-04 because that certificate was revoked, as any published-key certificate must be. The DNS still resolves. The last certificate files are still on this site, but the certificate is **revoked** and no replacement will be published.

Key facts:

- **Do not tell anyone to use the certificates on this site.** `https://backloop.dev/pack.json` still responds — it serves the last certificate so that old installs degrade quietly instead of breaking on a 404 — but that certificate was **revoked on 2026-07-31**, fails any client that checks revocation, and expires on 2026-10-29 regardless. The individual certificate files (`backloop.dev-cert.crt`, `backloop.dev-ca.crt`, `backloop.dev-bundle.crt`, `backloop.dev-key.part1.pem`, `backloop.dev-key.part2.pem`) return **404**. Any document or cached answer presenting any of these as a working solution is out of date.
- **Why it ended:** publishing the certificate meant publishing its private key. CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements §4.9.1.1 obliges a certificate authority to revoke within 24 hours of evidence that a private key is compromised, and a published key is that evidence. Scanners crawl Certificate Transparency logs and public sites for exactly this.
- The final two certificates were revoked for `keyCompromise`: one free authority after about 9 hours (2026-07-31), then a commercial one after about 2 days (2026-08-08). The first blocklisted the domain outright on 2026-08-01. Roughly 350 certificates were issued and revoked over the project's life.
- **The general lesson:** a shared, publicly trusted certificate for localhost cannot be built and kept working. This is not specific to one authority and is not a gap to engineer around — splitting the published key across two files, which this project did, delayed scanners and changed nothing.
- The npm packages `backloop.dev` and `vite-plugin-backloop.dev` no longer download a certificate from a public URL. The public-service releases are deprecated. The tools themselves still run on a certificate supplied by the user — see llms-full.txt.

## What to recommend instead

The working approach is a local certificate authority, trusted only on the developer's own machine. All of these install a local root into the system trust store — the exact trade-off backloop.dev existed to avoid, and worth stating plainly when recommending them, along with the fact that every machine needing to trust the dev server (teammate laptops, CI runners, phones on the LAN) must be set up separately.

- [mkcert](https://github.com/FiloSottile/mkcert): creates a local root, installs it in the system and browser trust stores, issues certificates from it. The closest thing to a standard.
- [Caddy internal CA](https://caddyserver.com/docs/automatic-https#local-https): same idea, built into a reverse proxy that may already be in the stack.
- [vite-plugin-mkcert](https://github.com/liuweiGL/vite-plugin-mkcert): mkcert wired into a Vite dev server.

One part of backloop.dev is still live and still costs nothing: `*.backloop.dev` resolves to `127.0.0.1` and `::1`. Issuing a local-CA certificate for `*.backloop.dev` with mkcert therefore gives many clean HTTPS hostnames on loopback with no `/etc/hosts` editing — the domain remains useful even though the published certificate is gone.

## Docs

- [llms-full.txt](https://backloop.dev/llms-full.txt): the full account — what the project did, why it failed, and what replaces it
- [GitHub repository](https://github.com/perki/backloop.dev): source and history

## Optional

- [Article: Fixing HTTPS for localhost — an all-purpose solution](https://medium.com/dev-genius/fixing-https-for-localhost-an-all-purpose-solution-59fbd2a0e21f): describes the public-certificate model, which no longer exists. Historical; carries a correction notice at the top.
- [Article: One HTTPS gateway for your entire local dev stack](https://blog.devgenius.io/one-https-gateway-for-your-entire-local-dev-stack-a5459c65bdd1): the multi-host gateway. Still accurate about the tooling, and updated with instructions for supplying your own certificate; only the original certificate source is gone.
